usage: the verb is 찍다 (to tap/stamp on the reader), never 누르다
I top up the transit card.
충전(充電) literally 'charge electricity' — reused for adding cash value
The transit card balance is low.
잔액 = remaining balance; the exact phrase the gate flashes
Can I use a transit card?
돼요? = 'does it work?', the polite way to ask a cabbie or shop
examples: 교통카드 있어요?
Do you have a transit card?
simplest form — just 있다 + the noun
편의점에서 교통카드를 충전했어요.
I topped up my transit card at the convenience store.
에서 marks where the action happens; CU/GS25 all do it
요즘은 지갑 없이 휴대폰으로 교통카드를 찍어요.
These days I tap the transit card with my phone instead of a wallet.
real mobile-T-money habit; 으로 = by means of the phone
nuance: 교통카드(交通+card) literally welds the Sino-Korean 교통 'traffic/transport' onto the English 'card', and names the rechargeable tap-to-ride card (T머니, 캐시비, or a 후불 credit card) for buses, the subway, and even some taxis. The make-or-break verb is 찍다 'to tap/stamp', never 누르다 'to press a button' — you lay the card flat on the reader, you don't push anything. A prepaid card you 충전 'top up' at convenience stores; the gate beeps your 잔액 'remaining balance'. Don't confuse it with a plain 카드, which to a Korean means a credit/debit card for shopping; the tap-to-ride one is always the full 교통카드. English 'swipe' also misleads — there is no magnetic swipe, only a contactless 찍다.

mistakes: Saying 교통카드를 눌러요 for tapping in.
누르다 means to press a button; you tap a card flat on the reader, which is 찍다. → 교통카드를 찍어요.
Using bare 카드 to mean the transit card.
To a Korean 카드 alone = a credit/debit card for buying things. The tap-to-ride card must be the full 교통카드 to be unambiguous.
Saying 교통카드를 채워요 for topping up.
채우다 = fill a physical container; money value on a card is 충전하다. → 교통카드를 충전해요.

usage: 끊다 'to cut' is the idiomatic verb for buying a ticket/pass
you reload the same card every period (30 days / 60 rides)
A commuter pass is cheaper than the regular fare.
the standard Seoul Metro period pass — subway only
examples: 정기권이 더 싸요?
Is a commuter pass cheaper?
simple yes/no comparison with 더 'more'
매일 지하철을 타니까 정기권을 끊었어요.
Since I take the subway every day, I bought a commuter pass.
니까 gives the reason; 끊다 = buy the pass
출퇴근만 생각하면 정기권이 이득인데 주말 외출이 많으면 손해예요.
For just commuting a pass pays off, but if you go out a lot on weekends it's a loss.
real cost trade-off; 인데 contrasts the two cases
nuance: 정기권(定期券) is built from 정기 'fixed period' (定 fix + 期 term) plus 권 'ticket/voucher', so literally a 'fixed-term ticket' — a period/commuter pass. The dividing line versus a single 일회용 ticket is repetition: 정기권 only pays off if you ride the same route daily, since Seoul's subway version is a 30-day, 60-trip card. The sharp trap is coverage — the standard subway 정기권 works on the subway ONLY: no buses, and crucially no free 환승 'transfer' to a bus, so a bus-leg commuter loses money. The verb is 끊다 (idiom, literally 'to cut', from tearing a paper ticket) or 충전하다 to reload. Contrast 정기권 (period-based) with 회수권, an older booklet of single fares bought by count, not by time.

structuredNuance.t: A period/commuter pass. It only pays off if you ride the same route daily, since Seoul's subway version is a 30-day, 60-trip card. The dividing line versus a single 일회용 ticket is repetition: 정기권 is period-based, 일회용 is a single trip. Also contrast 정기권 (period-based) with 회수권, an older booklet of single fares bought by count, not by time.

The verb is 끊다 (idiom, literally 'to cut', from tearing a paper ticket) or 충전하다 to reload.

mistakes: Assuming the subway 정기권 covers bus transfers.
The standard period pass is subway-only and gives no free bus 환승, unlike a normal 교통카드. Check your route's bus legs first.
Confusing 정기권 with a one-ride 일회용 ticket.
정기권 is time/count-based for repeat commuting; 일회용 is a single trip. Buying 정기권 for occasional travel wastes money.
Saying 정기권을 사요 and expecting it to sound native.
Korean idiomatically 'cuts' a ticket: 정기권을 끊다. 사다 is understood but 끊다 is what locals say.

usage: 놓치다 = to miss (let slip) a vehicle you meant to catch
means its DEPARTURE time, not arrival — leave early
I have to catch the last train.
The last train is gone (service has ended).
끊기다 = service is cut off for the night
examples: 막차가 몇 시예요?
What time is the last train?
bare schedule question, the survival phrase
막차 끊기기 전에 빨리 가자.
Let's hurry before the last train is gone.
기 전에 = 'before ~'; classic end-of-night line
막차 놓쳐서 결국 택시 타고 왔어요.
I missed the last train, so in the end I came by taxi.
아서 = cause→result; 결국 'in the end' adds the resignation
nuance: 막차 fuses the native prefix 막- 'last/final' with 차(車) 'vehicle', literally 'the last vehicle', and it dominates Korean nightlife because the subway stops near midnight and missing it means a pricey taxi. Its exact opposite is 첫차 'first vehicle'. Two collocations are everywhere: 막차 끊기다 'the last service is cut off (gone)' and 막차 놓치다 'miss the last one'. The key pitfall is the English verb 'miss' — Korean uses 놓치다 'let slip', NEVER 잃어버리다 'lose (an object)', so 막차를 잃어버렸어요 sounds like you misplaced a train. Also note 막차 시간 is the DEPARTURE time, so a learner who reads it as an arrival time will stroll up just as the doors close.

Also note 막차 시간 is the DEPARTURE time, so a learner who reads it as an arrival time will stroll up just as the doors close.
Its exact opposite is 첫차 'first vehicle'.
막차 fuses the native prefix 막- 'last/final' with 차(車) 'vehicle', literally 'the last vehicle'.
The English verb 'miss' — Korean uses 놓치다 'let slip', NEVER 잃어버리다 'lose (an object)', so 막차를 잃어버렸어요 sounds like you misplaced a train.

mistakes: Saying 막차를 잃어버렸어요 for missing the last train.
잃어버리다 = lose a physical object. Failing to catch a train is 놓치다. → 막차를 놓쳤어요.
Treating 막차 시간 as the arrival time.
It is the departure time of the final train. Arrive a few minutes early or you literally watch it leave.
Saying 막 차 with a space or as 마지막 차 in casual speech.
The fixed word is one token, 막차. 마지막 차 is grammatical but stilted; locals just say 막차.

english: first train / first bus of the day
usage: the earliest departure, ~5:30 a.m. on the subway
What time is the first train?
I go on the first train.
(으)로 = by means of / on the first run
examples: 첫차가 몇 시예요?
What time is the first train?
simplest schedule question with 몇 시
공항 가려고 첫차를 탔어요.
I took the first train to go to the airport.
(으)려고 = intention 'in order to'; classic early-flight reason
밤새우고 그냥 첫차로 집에 갔어요.
I stayed up all night and just went home on the first train.
밤새우다 'pull an all-nighter'; 으로 marks the means
nuance: 첫차 joins the native prefix 첫- 'first' with 차(車) 'vehicle' — 'the first vehicle' — and is the mirror image of 막차; the subway 첫차 typically rolls around 5:30 a.m. People catch it for early flights or after pulling an all-nighter (밤새우다). The verb 다니다 'to run/operate (regularly)' is the natural partner for when service runs. The English-speaker trap is spacing and a near-homophone: write 첫차 as ONE word (첫 차 with a space reads as 'first car' counting vehicles), and don't mix it up with 첫째 'the first one / firstly', which orders items, not departures. Also resist the calque 'first car' — in transit context 차 here means the scheduled run, not an automobile.

첫차 joins the native prefix 첫- 'first' with 차(車) 'vehicle' — 'the first vehicle'.

mistakes: Writing 첫 차 with a space.
Spaced, 첫 차 reads as 'the first car' (counting vehicles). The first scheduled train is the single word 첫차.
Confusing 첫차 with 첫째.
첫째 = 'the first one' / 'firstly' for ordering things or birth order. The day's first departure is 첫차.
Using 첫번 차 to mean the first train.
That is not idiomatic; the established lexical item is 첫차. Just say 첫차.

usage: 연착되다 (passive feel) is the most common form
the wording on station/airport notice boards
이다 lets the noun itself be the predicate
examples: 기차가 연착됐어요.
The train was delayed.
the base sentence; 되다 turns the noun into 'got delayed'
눈이 많이 와서 KTX가 30분 연착됐어요.
It snowed a lot, so the KTX was delayed 30 minutes.
아서 = cause→effect; weather is the usual culprit
연착 때문에 면접에 늦을 뻔했어요.
Because of the delay I almost ended up late to my interview.
때문에 = 'because of'; ㄹ 뻔했다 = 'almost (nearly happened)'
nuance: 연착(延着) is pure Sino-Korean — 延 'delay/extend' + 着 'arrive' — literally 'a delayed arrival', used for trains, buses, and flights, and it's the word on the 연착 안내 'delay notice' board. Standard verb forms are 연착되다 and 연착하다. The crucial contrast is 연착 versus 지각(遲刻): 연착 is a VEHICLE running behind schedule, whereas 지각 is a PERSON arriving late (to work, class). So 'I was late because the train was 연착' needs both words. The pitfall is reaching for plain 늦다 'to be late' for the vehicle — natural for a person, but for a scheduled train/flight the precise transit term is 연착되다. The opposite of 연착 is arriving 정시에 'on time'.

Reaching for plain 늦다 'to be late' for the vehicle — natural for a person, but for a scheduled train/flight the precise transit term is 연착되다.

mistakes: Using bare 늦다 for a vehicle running behind schedule.
늦다 fits a person; a scheduled train/flight uses 연착되다. → 기차가 연착됐어요, not 기차가 늦었어요 in formal contexts.
Confusing 연착 with 지각.
지각 = a person being late (to work/school). 연착 = a vehicle's delayed arrival. They are not interchangeable.
Saying 연착이 됐다 vs 연착됐다 inconsistently.
Both are heard, but the clean standard is 연착되다 / 연착했다. Avoid dropping the verb entirely except on signage like '10분 연착'.

usage: the faster train/line that skips minor stops
The express is faster than the local.
보다 = 'than'; 일반 is the all-stops local
The express doesn't stop at this station.
examples: 급행이 더 빨라요.
The express is faster.
simplest comparison with 더 'more'
급행을 타면 20분 빨리 가요.
If you take the express, you get there 20 minutes faster.
면 = 'if/when'; concrete time saved
이 역엔 급행이 안 서니까 일반 타고 가다가 갈아타세요.
The express doesn't stop here, so take the local and transfer along the way.
platform-level advice; 다가 = switch mid-action
nuance: 급행(急行) is Sino-Korean 急 'urgent/fast' + 行 'go', literally 'fast-going' — express service (Seoul Line 9, the GTX, some Korail lines) that skips smaller stations to save time. Its opposites are 완행(緩行) 'slow-going' or, more commonly today, 일반 'general/local' (all stops). The decisive collocation is 안 서다 'doesn't stop': the 급행 bypasses many stations, so before boarding you must confirm it 서다 'stops' at your destination. The classic English-speaker pitfall is mixing the noun 급행 'express service' with the adjective 급하다 'to be in a hurry/urgent' — same 急 root, but 급하다 describes a person's rush, not a train. People weigh the time saved against the 급행's heavier crowding.

Mixing the noun 급행 'express service' with the adjective 급하다 'to be in a hurry/urgent' — same 急 root, but 급하다 describes a person's rush, not a train.

mistakes: Boarding a 급행 without checking 정차역 (where it stops).
The express skips many stations. If it doesn't 서다 at yours, you overshoot. Confirm first: 급행이 ○○역에 서요?
Confusing 급행 with 급하다.
급행 = express service (a noun). 급하다 = to be in a hurry (an adjective about a person/situation). Don't say 저는 급행해요 for 'I'm in a rush'.
Assuming 급행 is always better.
It's faster but typically far more crowded (Line 9 급행 is infamous). For a short hop or a skipped station, 일반 can be smarter.

usage: on a bus; here 누르다 IS right — it's a real button
I get off at the next stop.
tag-off (tapping your card when getting off)
what unlocks the free bus 환승
Please exit through the back door.
examples: 다음 정류장에서 하차할게요.
I'll get off at the next stop.
ㄹ게요 = speaker's intention; polite and natural on a bus
내릴 때 카드를 안 찍으면 하차 처리가 안 돼요.
If you don't tap your card when getting off, the tag-off doesn't register.
면 = 'if'; why you must tag off
하차 벨을 미리 눌러야 기사님이 세워 줘요.
You have to press the bell in advance so the driver stops for you.
아야 = 'only if/must'; 줘요 shows the driver doing it for you
nuance: 하차(下車) is Sino-Korean 下 'down' + 車 'vehicle' — literally 'down from the vehicle' — the formal counterpart to 승차 'boarding'. In everyday speech people just say 내리다 'to get off'; 하차 shows up on signs, announcements, and the bus fare system. It matters most on buses, where a 하차 태그 (tapping your card on exit) is what grants the free 환승 'transfer', and you press the 하차 벨 to signal your stop (note: here 누르다 'press' is correct, because the bell really is a button). Exit norm is the 뒷문 'rear door'. The pitfall: don't over-formalize chatty speech — telling a friend 하차합니다 sounds like a PA announcer; just say 내려요.

structuredNuance.t: 'Down from the vehicle' — getting off. It matters most on buses, where a 하차 태그 (tapping your card on exit) is what grants the free 환승 'transfer', and you press the 하차 벨 to signal your stop (note: here 누르다 'press' is correct, because the bell really is a button). 하차(下車) is Sino-Korean 下 'down' + 車 'vehicle' — literally 'down from the vehicle'.
Don't over-formalize chatty speech — telling a friend 하차합니다 sounds like a PA announcer; just say 내려요.

mistakes: Skipping the 하차 태그 on the bus.
Without tapping off, the system can't compute distance and you lose the 환승 discount (or get charged a max fare). Always tag off.
Confusing 하차 with 승차.
하차 = getting OFF (下 down). 승차 = getting ON (乘 ride). Reversing them sends you the wrong way through the doors.
Saying 하차해요 to a friend in casual chat.
하차 is formal/announcement register. In daily talk use 내리다 → 다음에서 내려요. Save 하차 for signs and the fare system.

usage: 券 'ticket' — a single-ride ticket, NOT the card
I board through the front door.
(으)로 = via; the bus norm is front-door boarding
the term for a taxi illegally turning you down
examples: 앞문으로 승차하세요.
Please board through the front door.
simple instruction; mirrors 뒷문 하차
승차권을 미리 사 두면 편해요.
It's convenient to buy your ticket in advance.
아 두다 = do ahead for later; 승차권 = a single fare ticket
어젯밤에 택시 승차 거부를 당했어요.
Last night I got refused a ride by a taxi.
당하다 = suffer/be subjected to; a real late-night frustration
nuance: 승차(乘車) is Sino-Korean 乘 'ride/board' + 車 'vehicle' — literally 'mount the vehicle' — the formal partner of 하차, while casual speech just uses 타다 'to get on/ride'. You meet it in 승차권 'a fare ticket' (券 = ticket) and the well-known 승차 거부 'ride refusal', a taxi illegally declining a passenger (a genuine late-night problem). On buses the rule pairs up as 앞문 승차, 뒷문 하차 'board front, exit rear'. The pitfall is 승차권 vs 교통카드: 승차권 is a single paper/disposable ticket for one trip, whereas the reloadable tap card is a 교통카드 — calling your T-money a 승차권 is wrong. Also keep 승차 (boarding, the act) distinct from 탑승, which Koreans favor for boarding a plane/ship.

승차(乘車) is Sino-Korean 乘 'ride/board' + 車 'vehicle' — literally 'mount the vehicle'.
승차권 vs 교통카드: 승차권 is a single paper/disposable ticket for one trip, whereas the reloadable tap card is a 교통카드 — calling your T-money a 승차권 is wrong.

mistakes: Calling a 교통카드 a 승차권.
승차권 = a single-ride fare ticket (券). The rechargeable tap card is a 교통카드. They are different objects.
Confusing 승차 with 하차.
승차 = getting ON (乘 ride). 하차 = getting OFF (下 down). On buses it's 앞문 승차, 뒷문 하차 — don't swap them.
Using 승차 for boarding a plane.
For aircraft/ships Koreans usually say 탑승 (탑승 게이트, 탑승 시간). 승차 is for road/rail 車 vehicles.

usage: I go through the fare gate.
I tap my card at the gate.
에서 marks the place of the action
usually a low-balance or read error
Let's meet in front of the gate.
a default meet-up spot in any station
examples: 개찰구 앞에서 봐요.
See you in front of the fare gate.
the everyday meet-up line; 보다 here = 'meet/see'
잔액이 부족해서 개찰구가 안 열렸어요.
The gate wouldn't open because my balance was too low.
아서 = cause; the classic gate failure
개찰구를 통과하면 바로 승강장이 나와요.
Once you pass through the fare gate, the platform is right there.
면 = 'once/when'; 승강장 = the platform
nuance: 개찰구(改札口) is Sino-Korean 改 'check/examine' + 札 'ticket' + 口 'opening/gate' — literally a 'ticket-checking opening' — the subway/train fare gate where you 찍다 'tap' your 교통카드 to enter AND exit. If your 잔액 'balance' is too low it won't open and beeps at you, and it's one of the most common rendezvous points ('개찰구 앞에서 봐'). The platform beyond it is the 승강장. Two pitfalls: don't mix 개찰구 (the in-station fare gate) with 출입구 'a building's entrance/exit' (出入口) — both end in 口, but 출입구 is just a doorway with no fare. And remember to tap at BOTH the entry and exit gate; tap-in only can trigger a max-fare penalty.

structuredNuance.t: The subway/train fare gate where you 찍다 'tap' your 교통카드 to enter AND exit. If your 잔액 'balance' is too low it won't open and beeps at you, and it's one of the most common rendezvous points ('개찰구 앞에서 봐'). The platform beyond it is the 승강장. Remember to tap at BOTH the entry and exit gate; tap-in only can trigger a max-fare penalty.
Don't mix 개찰구 (the in-station fare gate) with 출입구 'a building's entrance/exit' (出入口) — both end in 口, but 출입구 is just a doorway with no fare.
개찰구(改札口) is Sino-Korean 改 'check/examine' + 札 'ticket' + 口 'opening/gate' — literally a 'ticket-checking opening'.

mistakes: Confusing 개찰구 with 출입구.
개찰구 = the fare gate inside a station (you tap to pass). 출입구 = a plain entrance/exit of a building. Different things despite the shared 口.
Tapping only when entering, not when exiting.
Distance-based fares need both taps. Skipping the exit tap at the 개찰구 can charge you the maximum fare. Tap in AND out.
Calling it a 게이트 and expecting full clarity.
게이트 is understood (esp. airport 탑승 게이트), but the standard subway word is 개찰구. Use 개찰구 for the fare gate.

usage: I look at the route map.
노선도 = route map (圖 'diagram'), the colored subway map
바뀌다 = (intransitive) get changed; route revisions happen
examples: 이 버스 노선이 우리 집 앞을 지나가요.
This bus route passes in front of my house.
지나가다 = pass by; a convenient route
처음 왔을 때 지하철 노선도가 너무 복잡해 보였어요.
When I first arrived, the subway route map looked so complicated.
아 보이다 = 'looks/seems'; the newcomer feeling
앱에서 노선이랑 막차 시간까지 다 확인할 수 있어요.
In the app you can check everything, even the route and the last-train time.
이랑 = casual 'and'; 까지 = 'even/up to'
nuance: 노선(路線) is Sino-Korean 路 'road' + 線 'line' — literally a 'road-line' — meaning a transit route/line for both buses and subways; the famous 노선도(路線圖) 'route map' (圖 = diagram) is the colored subway map newcomers squint at. The key usage split: for a specific subway line Koreans say the number + 호선 (2호선 'Line 2'), while 노선 is the general word for a route's path, used heavily for buses (버스 노선). Pitfalls: don't conflate 노선 'the route itself' with 노선도 'the map of routes' — one is the line, the other the diagram. And don't say 2노선 for Line 2; the counter is 호선. Apps like 카카오맵/네이버지도 list every 노선 and timetable.

mistakes: Saying 2노선 for 'Line 2'.
Subway lines use the counter 호선: 2호선, 9호선. 노선 is the generic 'route' word, mainly for buses. → 2호선.
Confusing 노선 with 노선도.
노선 = the route/line itself. 노선도 = the printed/onscreen map of routes (圖 diagram). Asking for a 노선 when you want the map gets you the wrong thing.
Using 길 for a bus route.
길 = a street/road or a way to walk. A scheduled transit route is 노선 (버스 노선), not 길.

usage: I change lines at the transfer station.
The next stop is a transfer station.
I get off at the transfer station.
에서 = at; then you switch lines
examples: 사당은 환승역이에요.
Sadang is a transfer station.
simplest A는 B예요 statement
사당에서 2호선으로 갈아타세요.
Transfer to Line 2 at Sadang.
(으)로 = the target line; giving directions
환승역은 걷는 거리가 길어서 갈아타는 데 시간이 좀 걸려요.
Transfer stations have long walking distances, so changing lines takes a while.
아서 = cause; 는 데 = 'in doing ~ it takes...'
nuance: 환승역(換乘驛) stacks three Sino-Korean roots — 換 'exchange' + 乘 'ride' + 驛 'station' — literally a 'ride-exchange station', a stop where two or more subway lines meet so you can 갈아타다 'transfer'. Big ones (사당, 신도림, 왕십리) are notoriously crowded with long underground walks. The sharp contrast is 환승역 vs 환승: 환승역 is the PLACE, while 환승 is the ACT/system of transferring — and a free subway↔bus 환승 depends on tapping your 교통카드 within the time limit, not merely on standing in a 환승역. Pitfalls: don't assume any station lets you switch lines (only a 환승역 does), and don't confuse 환승역 with 종점 'the terminal/last stop'. Note the native verb 갈아타다, not a borrowing, is what you actually 'do' here.

structuredNuance.t: A 'ride-exchange station', a stop where two or more subway lines meet so you can 갈아타다 'transfer'. Big ones (사당, 신도림, 왕십리) are notoriously crowded with long underground walks. Note the native verb 갈아타다, not a borrowing, is what you actually 'do' here.

The sharp contrast is 환승역 vs 환승: 환승역 is the PLACE, while 환승 is the ACT/system of transferring — and a free subway↔bus 환승 depends on tapping your 교통카드 within the time limit, not merely on standing in a 환승역. Also don't confuse 환승역 with 종점 'the terminal/last stop'.
환승역(換乘驛) stacks three Sino-Korean roots — 換 'exchange' + 乘 'ride' + 驛 'station' — literally a 'ride-exchange station'.
Don't assume any station lets you switch lines — only a 환승역 does.

mistakes: Assuming you can change lines at any station.
Only a 환승역 connects multiple lines. At a normal 역 you can't switch lines without exiting. Check that it's a 환승역.
Confusing 환승역 (place) with 환승 (act/system).
환승역 = the transfer STATION. 환승 = the transfer itself / the discount system. A free bus transfer needs a timely card tap, not just being in a 환승역.
Confusing 환승역 with 종점.
환승역 = a mid-route junction of lines. 종점 = the end-of-line terminal. They sit at very different points of a route.

english: terminal, last stop (end of the line)
usage: I get off at the last stop.
where a city bus route ends
I go all the way to the terminal.
까지 = up to/all the way to
examples: 여기가 종점이에요?
Is this the last stop?
simple confirmation question to the driver
깜빡 졸다가 종점까지 가 버렸어요.
I dozed off and ended up riding all the way to the last stop.
다가 = mid-action switch; 아 버리다 = regret it's done
종점에서 차고지로 들어가니까 다들 내리세요.
The bus heads into the depot from the last stop, so everyone please get off.
니까 = reason; the end-of-line notice
nuance: 종점(終點) is Sino-Korean 終 'end' + 點 'point' — literally the 'end point' — the final stop where a bus or subway route terminates, the opposite of 첫 정거장 'the first stop' (or 기점 'the origin point'). The driver announces 'here is the 종점, everyone off,' and dozing off to ride 종점까지 'all the way to the end' is a relatable mishap. The pitfall is 종점 vs 터미널: 종점 is the end of a LOCAL route (a city bus's last stop, often by a 차고지 'depot'), whereas a 터미널 (버스 터미널) is the big intercity hub where express coaches depart — calling Seoul's Express Bus 터미널 a 종점 is wrong. Also keep 종점 (end of route) apart from 환승역 (a mid-route junction); they're at opposite ends of the journey.

structuredNuance.t: The 'end point' — the final stop where a bus or subway route terminates, the opposite of 첫 정거장 'the first stop' (or 기점 'the origin point'). The driver announces 'here is the 종점, everyone off,' and dozing off to ride 종점까지 'all the way to the end' is a relatable mishap.

The pitfall is 종점 vs 터미널: 종점 is the end of a LOCAL route (a city bus's last stop, often by a 차고지 'depot'), whereas a 터미널 (버스 터미널) is the big intercity hub where express coaches depart — calling Seoul's Express Bus 터미널 a 종점 is wrong. Also keep 종점 (end of route) apart from 환승역 (a mid-route junction); they're at opposite ends of the journey.
종점(終點) is Sino-Korean 終 'end' + 點 'point' — literally the 'end point'.

mistakes: Calling an intercity bus 터미널 a 종점.
터미널 (버스 터미널/고속터미널) = the large hub where intercity coaches start. 종점 = the last stop of a local route, often near a depot. Don't substitute one for the other.
Confusing 종점 with 환승역.
종점 = the end of the line. 환승역 = a junction mid-route where you switch lines. They are at different points of a route.
Saying 마지막 역 and assuming it always equals 종점.
마지막 역 'the last station' is understood, but the fixed transit term for a route's end is 종점 (esp. for buses). Use 종점 for the end-of-line stop.
